====================================================================================================

# Power lab: where a 2014 MacBook Pro's battery goes

> **TL;DR.** A 2014 MacBook Pro idles at about 20 W on battery: backlight 5.0, display pipeline 4.4, CPU package 4.8, memory 1.7 and everything else about 4. The CPU package never reaches its deep sleep states (PC6/PC7) and the cause was not found. This page records what was measured, what each tried change saved, what was ruled out, two warnings, and how to use `power/power-lab`.

Related: [power/README](../power/README.md) · [SLEEP](SLEEP.md) · [FIELD-NOTES](FIELD-NOTES.md) · [GLOSSARY](GLOSSARY.md) · [INDEX](INDEX.md)

Findings from measuring a MacBookPro11,3 (15", mid-2014, Core i7-4870HQ, Intel Iris Pro + a switched-off NVIDIA GT 750M) running
Omarchy / Hyprland on kernel 7.2. Everything below was measured with `power/power-lab`, on battery, with the terminal idle.
The numbers are for this machine and this battery (about 75 % of its original capacity, 71 Wh when full); the method is general.

## Why the method matters

* **A busy terminal costs about 4 W by itself.** A working Claude window (animated spinner, streaming text) keeps the graphics chip
  and display engine awake: the Intel GPU idled only 48 % of the time and raised 128 display interrupts a second, against 100 % idle
  and 0 interrupts when the terminal was quiet. So every measurement is taken by a background service while the terminal is idle.
  `power-lab` re-launches itself that way after one sudo prompt.
* **Read the battery, not an estimate.** Draw = `current_now x voltage_now` from `/sys/class/power_supply/BAT0`, averaged over 20-35 s
  (single samples swing by +-3 W). Run on battery: the charger hides the draw.
* **Noise is about +-1 W.** Baselines taken minutes apart wandered between 14.9 and 16.2 W. A change below about 1 W needs repeating
  before it is believed.
* **Deep sleep is all-or-nothing.** The CPU package only enters its deep states when *every* blocker is cleared, so single changes can
  look like nothing even when they matter. That is why `power-lab stack` applies fixes cumulatively.

## Where the 20 W goes

| Piece | Watts | How it was isolated |
|---|---|---|
| Backlight at 73 % | about 5.0 | 20.0 W normal vs 15.0 W with the backlight at 0 |
| Display pipeline and panel electronics | about 4.4 | 15.1 W vs 10.7 W with the display switched off (`dpms disable`) |
| CPU package (cores, graphics, uncore) | about 4.8 | RAPL `package-0` counter, display on |
| Memory (DRAM) | about 1.7 | RAPL `dram` counter |
| The rest: fans at their floor, SSD, Wi-Fi, conversion losses | about 4 | what is left |

The CPU itself is 97 % idle and 99 % of that idle time is in core C7. The expensive part is the **package**: with the display on it
sits in the shallow state PC2 for about 90 % of the time, with the display off in PC3 (about 88 %), and **PC6/PC7 stayed at 0 % in
every test**. Deep package sleep would cut the package to roughly a quarter of its power.

## What was tried

Single changes, each reverted straight after (`power-lab singles`, noise about +-1 W):

| Change | Effect |
|---|---|
| Wi-Fi power saving on | **-0.94 W** (also -0.9 W in the cumulative run) |
| Fan floor lowered from about 2,100 to 1,200 rpm | -0.73 W (one run; needs repeating) |
| PCIe ASPM `powersave` | -0.21 W (ASPM was already on for most links) |
| Camera driver unloaded | +0.13 W (nothing) |
| SATA link power saving | 0.00 W |
| NMI watchdog off | +0.07 W |
| Sleep allowed for the SSD controller and the Intel ME | +0.46 W (noise) |

**Wi-Fi power saving is a trade-off, not free.** Omarchy ships `wifi.powersave = 2` (off) on purpose: power saving can add
20-300 ms latency spikes on idle links, and some Intel firmware drops the link when it naps. `power/install-wifi-powersave`
overrides that with a file that sorts later. On this machine (Broadcom wl, this router) replies on an idle link took 2.3-5.8 ms with
power saving on, with no spikes. The case that test cannot show is an unsolicited packet arriving while the card dozes (it can wait
up to about a beacon interval, roughly 100 ms): fine for chat and browsing, possibly noticeable in real-time games or calls.

Cumulative (`power-lab stack`, display on): baseline 15.3 W, all fixes 13.8 W, i.e. about 1.5 W, nearly all of it Wi-Fi power saving.
With the display off, every fix applied: 9.0 W against 9.4 W unfixed.

## What was ruled out

* **The CPU is not capped by the firmware.** `power/msr-probe`: package C-state limit C7s, register unlocked, no auto-demotion.
* **The discrete GPU is off.** The link is down; the kit keeps the real vga_switcheroo state in `/run/nvidia-off.status` because
  sysfs `power_state` reads D0 after a sleep even when the card is off.
* **PCIe link power saving is largely on already** (L0s/L1 enabled on most links). Off only for the camera and the Thunderbolt parts.

## What is still open

* **What blocks deep package sleep.** Not found. The hunt (`power-lab hunt`, 2026-10-07, display off) turned PCIe link power saving
  (L1) on for the FaceTime camera link: no change. The kernel **refused** to turn it on for the Thunderbolt bridge and controller
  (`06:00.0`, `08:00.0`), which sit directly behind the CPU's own PCIe port and are the strongest suspects, so that link is
  untested. Taking the camera, both audio controllers, the Intel management engine, the SMBus controller and the Wi-Fi card off the
  bus one after another also changed nothing: the package stayed at PC3 (86-90 %) and PC6/PC7 at 0 %. What is left (the SSD, the USB
  controller, the graphics chip, the Thunderbolt chain, the CPU/PCH links) cannot be removed safely. Worth up to about 3 W, but the
  remaining search is not worth the risk.
* **The display.** The graphics driver reports `FBC disabled: stolen memory not initialised`: Apple's firmware reserved no graphics
  memory, so the screen cannot be compressed and is read in full from RAM 60 times a second. There is no panel self-refresh either.
  That is a firmware limit, not a setting.
* **Fan floor** at 1,200 rpm: promising (-0.73 W, and quieter) but measured once.

## Two warnings from this work

**Never rescan or remove PCI devices on this machine.** After the device-removal steps of an early `hunt`, the cleanup wrote to
`/sys/bus/pci/rescan`. While re-attaching the devices the kernel hit a general protection fault inside the `intel_rapl_msr` module
(`rescan_store -> pci_bus_add_devices -> ... -> set_floor_freq_atom`). That killed the test script mid-cleanup, which left the display
switched off and the backlight at 0, and the kernel hung on the next suspend, so a hard reset was needed. Nothing was damaged (btrfs
reported no errors). `power-lab` no longer removes devices or rescans, and it now registers an `ExecStopPost` cleanup command with
systemd, which restores the display and the backlight however the test ends (tested: it runs even after the script segfaults).

**Do not unload the `thunderbolt` driver while its idle controller is allowed to runtime-sleep.** On this machine the reload failed
(`device inaccessible`, `timeout resetting host router`, probe error -22) and the Falcon Ridge controller vanished from the PCI bus
until the next reboot. The saving it offered (at most about 0.7 W) is below the noise, so `power-lab` no longer tests it.

## Using the tool

```
power/power-lab quiet --check     # look only: what it detected on this machine
power/power-lab quiet             # about 2 min
power/power-lab breakdown         # about 3 min, adds CPU-package power and package sleep states
power/power-lab singles           # about 9 min
power/power-lab stack             # about 9 min
power/power-lab hunt              # about 3 min, looks for what keeps the CPU package out of deep sleep (works on the charger)
power/power-lab results [mode]    # show the last results (data/power-lab/, not committed)
power/power-lab <mode> --check    # look only: what it detected, change nothing
```

Keep the charger unplugged and your hands off the keyboard and trackpad while a test runs (input wakes the display). The screen goes
dark for a few minutes and comes back by itself. Nothing is permanent: each change is reverted right after its measurement and on any
exit; the backlight and display are restored at the end. The test runs as a systemd service whose cleanup step (`power-lab rescue`, never typed by hand) runs after it ends for any reason, even a crash.

---

# sleep/: lid, sleep and hibernate on the MacBookPro11,3

> **TL;DR.** On this Mac, deep sleep (S3) never wakes when the lid opens. These scripts switch to **light sleep** (s2idle), which wakes at
> once, make **hibernate** stay off, let a plain hibernate ask for **one** password, and **record** what every sleep did and cost.
> Every installer takes `--remove`; `--help` only prints usage. The full story with measurements: [docs/SLEEP.md](../docs/SLEEP.md).

| Script | Root? | What it does | Undo |
|---|---|---|---|
| `install-s2idle` | sudo | a tmpfiles rule `w /sys/power/mem_sleep - - - - s2idle`, applied early at every boot | `--remove` (sets `deep` again) |
| `install-hibernate-mode` | sudo | `HibernateMode=shutdown` in `/etc/systemd/sleep.conf.d/10-hibernate-shutdown.conf`: save the image, then power off instead of restarting | `--remove` |
| `install-hibernate-nolock` | no | points the user service `omarchy-sleep-lock` at a shim (`~/.local/share/omarchy-kit/sleep-lock-shim`) so a plain hibernate skips the lock screen. Refuses if Omarchy's sleep monitor is missing or changed, or if the resume device is not on an encrypted volume | `--remove` |
| `sleep-lock-policy` | n/a | what the shim runs: skips the lock **only** when logind's newest line is exactly `The system will hibernate now!`; anything else, or any error, runs Omarchy's real lock (falling back to `omarchy-system-lock`, then `loginctl lock-session`). `--check` prints `hibernate` or `lock` | n/a |
| `install-battery-log` + `battery-log` | sudo | a hook in `/usr/lib/systemd/system-sleep/` (the only folder this systemd reads) that logs the battery charge before and after every sleep (journal tag `sleep-battery`) | `--remove` |
| `sleep-check` | no | reads the journal: every suspend and hibernate, its mode, how long, how much battery; `--json` for the Setup log | read-only |
| `acpi-prw-scan` | no | research tool: reads raw DSDT/SSDT tables and prints every `_PRW` wake definition with its device path | read-only |

## Use

```bash
sudo sleep/install-s2idle                # lid wakes the Mac again
sudo sleep/install-hibernate-mode        # hibernate stays off
sleep/install-hibernate-nolock           # one password after hibernate (no root; read the trade-off in docs/SLEEP.md first)
sudo sleep/install-battery-log           # then: sleep/sleep-check shows what each sleep cost
sleep/sleep-check                        # the report
```

## Trade-offs you should know

Light sleep keeps the fans spinning and drains the battery faster than deep sleep. Skipping the lock before hibernate leaves the screen unlocked
for the ~30 s the image takes to save, and unlocked if a hibernate ever fails. Both are explained, with the open decision about the lid, in
[docs/SLEEP.md](../docs/SLEEP.md).

## Checked by

Setup log rows **Sleep and wake with the lid**, **Hibernate powers off and stays off**, **One password after hibernate**, **Battery log around sleep**; tests in
`test/test_sleep_power_themes.py` (every installer in a sandbox with fake commands).

---

FILE: power/README.md  (power/ scripts)

# power/: where the battery goes, and what to do about it

> **TL;DR.** The profile follows the charger, Wi-Fi can nap between packets (about 0.9 W), and `power-lab` measures where the roughly 20 W of an idle
> MacBook goes, trying power-saving changes one at a time and undoing each. The findings (including what was ruled out and what is still open) are in
> [docs/POWER-LAB.md](../docs/POWER-LAB.md).

| Script | Root? | What it does | Undo |
|---|---|---|---|
| `power-auto` (+ `power-auto.service`) | no | switches the power profile when the charger changes: performance on AC, balanced on battery (override in `~/.config/omarchy-kit/power-auto.conf`); `--once`, `--status` | `install-power-auto --remove` |
| `install-power-auto` | no | installs the user service | `--remove` |
| `install-wifi-powersave` | sudo | `/etc/NetworkManager/conf.d/wifi-powersave.conf` with `wifi.powersave = 3`; overrides Omarchy's deliberate "off"; a packet can wait up to one beacon interval (about 100 ms) | `--remove` |
| `power-lab` | asks for sudo once | modes `quiet`, `breakdown`, `singles`, `stack`, `hunt`, plus `results` and `<mode> --check`. Runs as a transient systemd service so the terminal stays idle (a busy terminal adds about 4 W); every change is reverted right after its measurement and on any exit, by a cleanup step that systemd runs after the test (`power-lab rescue`, never typed by hand) | nothing permanent |
| `msr-probe` | root, read-only | prints the CPU's package C-state limit and related switches | read-only |

## Use

```bash
power/install-power-auto                 # profile follows the charger
sudo power/install-wifi-powersave        # about -0.9 W, see the trade-off above
power/power-lab quiet --check            # look only: what it detected on this machine
power/power-lab breakdown                # about 3 minutes, charger unplugged, hands off the keyboard
power/power-lab results                  # the last results (data/power-lab/, not committed)
```

## Rules learned here

Keep the charger unplugged during a test (the draw is read from the battery); measure with the terminal idle; never remove or rescan PCI devices
(a rescan crashed the kernel); never unload the `thunderbolt` driver. See [docs/FIELD-NOTES.md](../docs/FIELD-NOTES.md).

## Checked by

Setup log rows **Power profile follows the charger**, **Wi-Fi power saving (about 0.9 W less)**; tests in `test/test_sleep_power_themes.py`.

# gpu/: keep the hot NVIDIA GPU off

> **TL;DR.** The MacBookPro11,3 has an Intel GPU and a hot NVIDIA GT 750M that `nouveau` never lets sleep (about 70 °C, fans near 5,900 rpm).
> `nvidia-off` powers it down through `vga_switcheroo` at boot and after every sleep; fans settle near 2,100 to 2,200 rpm.
> All scripts refuse to run on any other model.

| Script | Root? | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `nvidia-off` (+ `nvidia-off.service`) | root (runs as a service) | writes OFF to `vga_switcheroo` for the NVIDIA card; skipped when an external display is connected or the card is in use; never writes ON; copies the real state to `/run/nvidia-off.status` |
| `gpu-status` | no | which GPU drives the screen, the real vga_switcheroo state, and what the firmware boots with |
| `switch-to-intel` | sudo | sets Apple's `gpu-power-prefs` firmware variable so the panel is on Intel from power-on (takes effect next boot; recovery steps are in the script header) |
| `switch-to-nvidia` | sudo | removes that variable (the firmware default) |

## Install and undo

```bash
sudo install -m755 gpu/nvidia-off /usr/local/bin/ && sudo install -m644 gpu/nvidia-off.service /etc/systemd/system/ && sudo systemctl enable nvidia-off.service
sudo systemctl disable --now nvidia-off.service        # undo for good
echo ON | sudo tee /sys/kernel/debug/vgaswitcheroo/switch   # undo right now
```

Pitfall: sysfs `power_state` for the card can read D0 after a sleep even when it is off; trust `gpu-status`, not sysfs ([FIELD-NOTES](../docs/FIELD-NOTES.md)).

## Checked by

Setup log rows **Screen on the efficient Intel GPU**, **Idle NVIDIA GPU powered off**.

---

# audio/: speaker EQ that bypasses itself for headphones

> **TL;DR.** The 2014 MacBook speakers get a voicing EQ (a high-pass, a warmth boost, a de-boxing cut, a presence cut, some air) installed in Omarchy's
> speaker-tuning layout. A watcher sends only the speakers through it. It is unmeasured voicing for small laptop drivers, not a measured correction.

| File | What |
|---|---|
| `design_eq.py` | computes the exact response of the biquad chain and the pre-gain that keeps it at or below -0.5 dB (no limiter needed); writes `eq_design.json` and `macbookpro11-speakers.conf` |
| `macbookpro11-speakers.conf` | the PipeWire filter-chain settings that `design_eq.py` generates |
| `install-speaker-eq` | no root: installs the tuning in `~/.config/pipewire/` and the user services; re-run after editing `design_eq.py`; `--remove` undoes it (`omarchy-audio-tuning off`) |
| `speaker-eq-follow` (+ `.service`) | speakers and headphones are two ports of one hardware sink, so this points the default output at the EQ for speakers and straight at the hardware for headphones; it leaves Bluetooth and HDMI choices alone |

The tuning talks to RTKit directly (`rtportal.enabled = false`): the desktop portal reported a 0 us realtime budget here and the kernel killed the audio thread.

Checked by: Setup log rows **Speaker EQ, bypassed for headphones**, **Realtime audio priority (rtkit)**.

# boot/: a faster, themed boot

> **TL;DR.** The Limine menu waits 1 s instead of 5 (any key still opens the full menu, snapshots included), shows a wallpaper in the current Omarchy theme, and uses the
> theme's colours. Plymouth is told to draw on the firmware framebuffer (`UseSimpledrm=1`), so the splash and the disk-passphrase prompt appear about 0.5 s
> into the kernel instead of about 3 s, and the boot image is rebuilt the way Omarchy does (`limine-mkinitcpio`).

| Script | What |
|---|---|
| `make-wallpaper` | no root: makes the boot wallpaper (`omarchy-boot.png`) and colours (`boot-colors.env`) from the *current* Omarchy theme; re-run after switching themes |
| `apply-boot-look` | root: edits only the header of `/boot/limine.conf` (the entries below belong to `limine-update`), sets Plymouth `UseSimpledrm=1`, and rebuilds the boot image; `--undo` restores the backups |

`sudo boot/apply-boot-look`, then reboot. Setup log row: **Faster, themed boot screen**.

FILE: backup/README.md  (backup/ scripts)

# backup/: a Time Machine for your files

> **TL;DR.** Two layers. Hourly local snapshots of `/home` with snapper (needs btrfs; keeps the last 6 hours, 7 days, 2 weeks and 1 month; browse or restore any
> file without sudo), and Pika Backup (a friendly borg GUI) for the real, encrypted, scheduled backup to an external drive or a server. Snapshots live on the *same*
> disk: they undo mistakes, not a dead disk.

`sudo backup/install-backups` (preview with `--dry-run`, which needs no sudo) installs both; afterwards open Pika Backup and pick the drive, the one step that needs
you. `sudo backup/install-backups --remove` removes the `/home` snapper config and the timeline timer (snapshots already taken stay until you delete them; Pika Backup
stays installed). Setup log rows: **Hourly snapshots of /home**, **A real backup of your files to an external drive (Pika Backup)**.

---

Related: [docs/MAC-FEEL](../docs/MAC-FEEL.md) · [docs/INDEX](../docs/INDEX.md)

FILE: docs/MAC-FEEL.md  (Mac feel)
====================================================================================================

# Making Omarchy feel like a Mac

> **TL;DR.** Everything the kit changes so a macOS user feels at home: right-Option accents, a real Caps Lock, ⌘ shortcuts in apps (⌘ as Ctrl everywhere was tried and removed), the macOS icons and pointer, a Dock, a ⌘Tab app switcher, Mission Control, a Mac menu bar, the Golden Gate themes, three-finger behaviour, the power profile following the charger, a menu-bar clock with the date, Auto appearance, working sleep and hibernate, Wi-Fi saving and six themes. Each row says where it lives, how it was verified and how to undo it; the decisions that still wait for a person follow.

Related: [GOLDEN-GATE](GOLDEN-GATE.md) · [look/README](../look/README.md) · [keys/README](../keys/README.md) · [icons/README](../icons/README.md) · [dock/README](../dock/README.md) · [menubar/README](../menubar/README.md) · [trackpad/README](../trackpad/README.md) · [appearance/README](../appearance/README.md) · [SLEEP](SLEEP.md) · [THEMES](THEMES.md) · [INDEX](INDEX.md)

What the kit changes so a macOS user feels at home on this MacBook, how each piece was checked, how to undo it, and
what is still waiting for a person. The live version of this (with real-time status) is the **Setup log** page.

## Done and verified

| Change | Where | Verified | Undo |
|---|---|---|---|
| Accents on the **right Option key** (⌥e e = é, ⌥n n = ñ, ⌥1 = ¡, ⌥⇧/ = ¿); left ⌥ stays Alt | `kb_variant = "mac"` in `input.lua` | every key checked with libxkbcommon | delete the line, `hyprctl reload`, restart fcitx5 |
| **13 ⌘ shortcuts** in apps (⌘A ⌘Z ⇧⌘Z ⌘R ⇧⌘R ⌘N ⇧⌘T ⌘D ⌘B ⌘I ⌘U ⌘[ ⌘]); terminals skipped | `keys/` | `test/verify-mackeys.mjs`: 32 checks against a real Brave window | `keys/install-mackeys --remove` |
| **Caps Lock is a real Caps Lock**: it capitalises, the light follows it, Shift does not cancel it. Removed: Omarchy's Compose key on Caps Lock, and Caps Lock on both Shifts (right Option still types every accent) | a marked block in `input.lua` (`keys/caps-lock`; the file as it was is kept as `input.lua.bak-caps`) | `hyprctl` shows `kb_options` empty on every keyboard; libxkbcommon compiles `<CAPS>` as `Caps_Lock` with plain Shift keys (before: `Multi_key` and Shift+Shift); `test/test_keyd.py`; not with a physical press | `keys/caps-lock compose` |
| **Mac icons and pointer**: the WhiteSur icon theme (a free re-drawing of the macOS icon style, not Apple's art) and an open-source macOS cursor set; the icon variant follows each Omarchy theme's light or dark mode | `icons/` (no root; downloads two pinned releases, checksums verified) | install on the real desktop, a real theme round trip (`mecha-unit`, `flexoki-light`, back), screenshots; `test/test_macdesktop.py` | `icons/install-icons --remove` |
| **A Dock** at the bottom: magnification, running dots, bounce on launch, right-click menu, Downloads and Trash, autohide (⌥⌘D), tinted glass that follows the Omarchy theme | `dock/` (a small Quickshell program, no root) | screenshots of the real compositor, pointer hover, autohide, a light and a dark theme, a real web app; idle cost 0.1 % of one core; `test/test_macdesktop.py`. Not verified: mouse clicks, start at login | `dock/install-dock --remove` (your `dock.json` stays) |
| **⌘Tab app switcher**: running apps, most recently used first; Tab to step, let go of ⌘ to switch; Q quits and H hides the selected app. Replaces *Next / Previous workspace* on Super+Tab (moved to Super+Ctrl+Shift+Right / Left) | `dock/` | real switcher over three apps; Tab, Return, and Ctrl or Super release driven with `wtype` while it had the keyboard; the Lua routing of ⌘Q with the switcher open or closed. Not verified: the real Super+Tab key chord | `dock/install-dock --remove` |
| **Mac menu bar**: Apple-style menu, the focused app's name in bold, File / Edit / View / Window / Help; workspaces in the middle, clock last on the right. The menus send the matching ⌘ shortcut to the focused app (almost no Wayland app publishes a real menu) | `menubar/` (a bar widget plugin and a Hyprland module, no root) | screenshots in both themes, a menu opened and an item run (File > New Window opened a window); layout moved and restored exactly in tests | `menubar/install-menubar --remove` (puts your layout back) |
| **Mission Control and App Exposé**: F3 (the Mac keyboard's Mission Control key, which did nothing), Super+Ctrl+Up or four fingers up open a Spaces bar and real pictures of the windows; Super+Ctrl+Down shows the focused app's windows. F4 (the Launchpad key, also dead before) opens the Apps menu | `dock/` | real windows on three spaces: previews of visible and non-visible spaces, Esc, arrows, Return into another space, closing a window, the + card, App Exposé; idle cost unchanged. Not verified: the real F3/F4 presses and the swipe | `dock/install-dock --remove` |
| **UI font, window buttons on the left, glass switch**: the bar, menus and Dock in Adwaita Sans (a free relative of San Francisco), the close button of GTK apps at the top left, and a switch for blur behind the glass (off) | `look/` (no root; one shell restart) | the whole bar redrawn with every icon intact (screenshot); the font rule tested to change quickshell's monospace and nothing else; `test/test_macsweep.py`. Not verified: the button layout in a real Files window | `look/install-look --remove` |
| **Golden Gate and Golden Gate Night themes**: macOS system-colour palettes (contrast-checked), rounded windows with soft shadows and a hairline edge, translucent rounded menus, launcher and notifications with the accent-blue selection, sliding spaces, original bridge wallpapers. Installed, **not applied** | `themes/` (no root) | applied on the real desktop in both variants (no Hyprland errors; terminal, notification, menus, launcher, Mission Control and the Dock screenshotted), then your theme was put back | `omarchy theme set "Mecha Unit"`; `themes/install-themes --remove golden-gate golden-gate-night` |
| **Three fingers**: swipe between spaces (default) or drag, never both | `THREE_FINGERS` in `input.lua` | trackpad page test in both modes | `trackpad/three-fingers swipe` |
| **Power profile follows the charger** | `power/` (user service, no root) | simulated charger against the real power daemon | `power/install-power-auto --remove` |
| **Menu-bar clock with the date** (Wed 7 Oct 15:08) | `omarchy bar set omarchy.clock format …` | screenshot of the bar | `omarchy bar set omarchy.clock format "dddd HH:mm"` |
| **Auto appearance** (light by day, dark at night), installed but **off** | `appearance/` | schedule logic for every hour, one real theme round trip | `auto-appearance off` |
| **Light sleep on the lid** (s2idle): closing the lid sleeps, opening it wakes at once | `sleep/install-s2idle` (a tmpfiles rule) | three real lid tests, awake again about 1.3 s after opening | `sudo sleep/install-s2idle --remove` |
| **Hibernate that stays off**: saves the session, powers off like a shutdown | `sleep/install-hibernate-mode` (`HibernateMode=shutdown`) | a real hibernate: it stayed off until the power button | `sudo sleep/install-hibernate-mode --remove` |
| **One password after hibernate** (no lock screen before a plain hibernate; only the disk passphrase) | `sleep/install-hibernate-nolock` (no root; refuses on an unencrypted disk) | a real hibernate: one password; suspend still locks | `sleep/install-hibernate-nolock --remove` |
| **Sleep battery log** around every sleep | `sleep/install-battery-log` (hook in `/usr/lib/systemd/system-sleep/`) | entries in the journal after real sleeps | `sudo sleep/install-battery-log --remove` |
| **Sleep check** from the journal: every suspend and hibernate, its mode, duration and battery use | `sleep/sleep-check` | run against this machine's real journal and tested on fake ones | read-only, nothing to undo |
| **Wi-Fi power saving** (about 0.9 W; a packet can wait up to one beacon interval) | `power/install-wifi-powersave` (overrides Omarchy's default off) | measured with `power/power-lab`; idle link latency 2.3 to 5.8 ms | `sudo power/install-wifi-powersave --remove` |
| **Six themes of our own**: Kawaii Bow, Mecha Unit, Solarpunk, each in two variants (CC BY 4.0; wallpapers drawn at install time) | `themes/install-themes` (no root; never touches other themes) | each applied to the live desktop and screenshotted; text contrast at least 4.5:1 | `themes/install-themes --remove` |

Everything is reversible and logged, with its undo command, on the Setup log page.

## Waiting for a person

- **Decide the lid plan.** Today closing the lid uses light sleep, which wakes instantly but keeps the fans spinning and drains the
  battery faster. The alternative, light sleep first and hibernate after about 15 minutes (`suspend-then-hibernate`), costs a
  second password on that automatic path. Not installed; see [SLEEP.md](SLEEP.md).
- **Measure a closed lid on battery**: unplug, close the lid for 10 minutes or more, open it, run `sleep/sleep-check`. The first
  8 W reading was too short to trust.
- **Retest the fan floor** at 1,200 rpm (one run saved about 0.7 W; it needs repeating before it is worth applying).
- **Type with your own fingers** the accents, ⌘ shortcuts and trackpad gestures; the Learn lessons check them.
- **Unplug the charger once** to see the power profile flip to `balanced`.
- **Backups** (needs a password): `sudo backup/install-backups` (preview with `--dry-run`) sets up hourly `/home`
  snapshots and installs Pika Backup. Snapshots on the same disk undo mistakes, not a dead disk, so also point Pika
  Backup at an external drive.
- **Try the real keys** for the Dock and switcher (a real keyboard is needed; the tests could only send virtual keys): hold ⌘ and press Tab a few times, then let go; Super+Q with the switcher open; F3, F4, Super+Ctrl+Up and Down and a four-finger swipe up; log out and in to see the Dock start by itself; click, right-click and drag over the Dock and the menu bar titles. What to expect is in [dock/README](../dock/README.md) and [menubar/README](../menubar/README.md).
- **Decide whether you still want ⌘ as Ctrl everywhere** (tried and removed on 2026-10-23; see the section below). Today both ⌘ keys are Super.
- **A decision about ⌘W ⌘T ⌘F ⌘S ⌘L ⌘G ⌘P**, below (not needed if you install the keyd layer: they are plain Ctrl in apps then).
- Optional: turn on Auto appearance (`auto-appearance on`).

## The decision: Mac keys that Omarchy already uses

Omarchy uses Super+W/T/F/S/L/G/P for window management, so those ⌘ shortcuts still need Ctrl inside apps. Each can be
switched on separately (`keys/mac-key-extras W T F S`). A key that is on sends Ctrl+key **in apps**; **in terminals** it
keeps its Omarchy meaning; and the Omarchy action stays reachable in every window at a new chord:

| Key | Mac meaning (in apps) | Omarchy meaning (kept in terminals) | Omarchy action in apps |
|---|---|---|---|
| W | close tab / window | close window | Super+Alt+W |
| T | new tab | toggle floating / tiling | Super+Alt+T |
| F | find | full screen | Super+Ctrl+Alt+F |
| S | save | toggle scratchpad | Super+Ctrl+Alt+S |
| L | address bar | toggle workspace layout | Super+Alt+L |
| G | find next | toggle window grouping | Super+Ctrl+Alt+G |
| P | print | pseudo window | Super+Ctrl+Alt+P |

**Recommendation:** W, T, F and S. They are the four a Mac user reaches for most, and what they displace is used far
less (a four-finger swipe down still toggles the scratchpad). L, G and P are rarer on both sides, so leave them until
they are missed.

## Tried and removed: the ⌘ key as Ctrl everywhere (keyd)

**Outcome (2026-10-23).** `keys/install-keyd` was installed and removed the same day. The left ⌘ became Ctrl while the right ⌘ stayed Super, and the owner wanted both ⌘ keys to behave alike, as the two Ctrl keys do. And keyd's own log showed that it
had **matched and grabbed the Apple trackpad** (`bcm5974`) although the config used the keyboard-only `k:` id; keyd warned that mouse movement was likely to break, and pointer behaviour was not tested before the removal. Both ⌘ keys are Super again and nothing of the layer remains
(the `keyd` package is still installed, disabled, with no configuration). Lesson: the daemon's device matching could only be tested with fakes before the install; any redo must exclude the trackpad by its full id, make both ⌘ keys identical and be checked in `journalctl -u keyd`.
What follows describes the design as it was prepared.

`keys/install-keyd` (one sudo command; `--dry-run` previews it) makes the **left ⌘ key act as Ctrl for every key in every app**, so every shortcut, ⌘-click and ⌘-scroll work, which the Hyprland
binds above cannot do. Mac system chords (⌘Space, ⌘Tab, ⌘`, ⌘Q, ⌘H, ⌘M, ⇧⌘3/4/5, ⌃⌘Q, ⌃⌘Space, ⌃⌘F) reach Hyprland as Super chords; ⌘←/→ are Home/End and ⌥←/→ move by words; Caps Lock needs a
deliberate 150 ms press. A terminal never receives ⌘ as Ctrl+letter: a small root service, `keyd-appmap`, reads Hyprland's terminal tag and switches the overlay (⌘C copies, ⌘D and ⌘Z do nothing).
Ctrl, Option, the **right ⌘ key** (still Super: all of Omarchy's shortcuts keep working on it), other keyboards and the trackpad are untouched.

- **The price.** The left ⌘ key no longer starts Omarchy's Super+Return or Super+1…9; use the right ⌘ key, or the trackpad gestures for spaces.
- **Safety.** If the keyboard ever misbehaves, Backspace + Escape + Enter together make keyd quit. The installer runs keyd's own checker before activating anything, refuses if another keyd configuration exists,
  and is undone by `sudo keys/install-keyd --remove`. If the service is down, ⌘C and ⌘V fall back to Ctrl+Insert and Shift+Insert, which terminals accept.
- **Why not the keyd group.** It would make every process in your session root-equivalent; the service runs as root instead, sandboxed.
- **Verified:** keyd 2.6.0's own checker on every configuration the generator writes; 17 tests drive keyd's real engine (compiled from its source) with key events and compare the keys that come out; the service against fake
  Hyprland sockets and its focus query against the live compositor; the installer as fake root in a namespace; the unit with `systemd-analyze verify`. **Not verified:** the daemon on the physical keyboard (needs root), how
  the keys feel, and whether 150 ms matches a real Mac's Caps Lock delay (Apple does not publish it).
- Details, the full chord table and the limits: [keys/README](../keys/README.md).

## Looked at and left alone

- **System font.** GTK apps and `system-ui` pages already use Adwaita Sans (GNOME's UI font, derived from Inter, the
  closest free relative of San Francisco). The stack most sites use (`-apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont`) falls to
  Liberation Sans, and fontconfig cannot change that in Chromium, which ignores substitutes that are not
  metric-compatible. Omarchy's generic `sans-serif` is a deliberate choice, so it was not overridden.
- **Optimized Battery Charging (80% limit).** The battery exposes no charge-limit control to Linux.
- **Press-and-hold accent picker.** No general equivalent on Linux; the right Option key does the same job.
- **A Dock** was left alone in the first pass (it fights the tiling idea) and has since been built, because it is the most recognisable part of the Mac desktop: [dock/](../dock/README.md). It
  is a Quickshell program rather than `nwg-dock-hyprland`, because the Mac Dock's magnification and the shared switcher need one program that knows what is running. It can be hidden (⌥⌘D, or `autohide` in its settings).
- **Blur behind the glass** (what "Liquid Glass" is) is built but **off**, on evidence: see [the measurement below](#blur-behind-the-glass).
- **Window corners and shadows** are in the Golden Gate themes and the UI font in `look/`. **Left alone:** the glossy traffic-light buttons (the apps draw their own), Apple's fonts, system sounds and layered icons (Apple's own work). [GOLDEN-GATE](GOLDEN-GATE.md) has the whole comparison.

## Blur behind the glass

Liquid Glass is translucency plus blur. `look/mac-glass on` turns on Hyprland's blur for the shell's own surfaces (Dock, switcher, Mission Control, menus, notifications, launcher, the bar's drop-downs; never the bar itself or the windows). It was measured, not guessed:
the same scripted workload ran with blur off and on, sampling the Intel GPU's actual clock ten times a second and the CPU time of Hyprland and Quickshell (two runs each, on the charger, the other
work on the machine unchanged).

| Workload | Blur | GPU busy | GPU mean clock | Hyprland CPU | Quickshell CPU |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| idle, 20 s | off | 10 % | 225 MHz | 14.6 % of a core | 0.5 % |
| idle, 20 s | on | 40 % | 320 MHz | 15.7 % | 0.5 % |
| app switcher x25 | off | 43 % | 370 MHz | 13.8 % | 8.6 % |
| app switcher x25 | on | 62 % | 725 MHz | 16.9 % | 9.7 % |
| Dock hover x6 | off | 27 % | 266 MHz | 7.7 % | 1.8 % |
| Dock hover x6 | on | 65 % | 353 MHz | 8.1 % | 2.0 % |
| notifications x8 | off | 27 % | 257 MHz | 13.3 % | 2.8 % |
| notifications x8 | on | 47 % | 669 MHz | 17.6 % | 2.5 % |

"GPU busy" is the share of samples above the idle clock. **Reading:** blur quadruples the idle GPU activity and roughly doubles the GPU clock whenever a glass surface moves, with Hyprland spending 5 to 30 % more CPU. The package's energy counter needs root, so
**battery draw was not measured**: the honest conclusion is "it costs, and on this laptop that has meant heat", not a number of watts. It is off by default. Turn it on, look at the fans and the battery for a day, and decide: `look/mac-glass on`, `look/mac-glass off`.
The surfaces are translucent and tinted without it (and the switcher and menus nearly opaque so text behind them cannot be read through them).

## Tests

```bash
node test/verify-portal.mjs      # needs the kit service running; every page, lessons, language switch
node test/verify-trackpad.mjs
node test/verify-keyboard.mjs
node test/verify-mackeys.mjs     # needs a Hyprland session; launches its own scratch Brave and cleans up
CDP_ATTACH=9334 node test/verify-trackpad.mjs   # same, in a real GPU Brave (use a full-size window)
```

FILE: keys/README.md  (keys/ scripts)
====================================================================================================

# keys/: Mac ⌘ shortcuts, the keyd command layer and Caps Lock

> **TL;DR.** Two ways to get your ⌘ shortcuts. `mackeys.lua` (no root) turns a list of Super+key chords into the Ctrl chord the focused app expects. `install-keyd`
> (needs sudo) goes all the way: the left ⌘ key acts as Ctrl for every key in every app, ⌘Tab, ⌘Space and ⌘Q reach Hyprland as Super chords, a terminal never receives ⌘ as
> Ctrl+letter, and the right ⌘ key stays Super for Omarchy's own shortcuts. `caps-lock` makes Caps Lock a real Caps Lock. If the keyboard ever misbehaves under keyd,
> press **Backspace + Escape + Enter** together and keyd quits.

> **Status (2026-10-23): `install-keyd` was tried and removed; do not install it as it is.** On the real laptop it made the left ⌘ act as Ctrl while the right ⌘ stayed Super, which the owner rejected (both ⌘ keys must behave alike,
> as the two Ctrl keys do), and keyd's log showed it had matched and **grabbed the Apple trackpad** (`bcm5974`) despite the keyboard-only `k:` id. A redo needs both ⌘ keys identical and the trackpad excluded by its full id, and must be checked
> in `journalctl -u keyd` before it is called done. `caps-lock` and `mackeys.lua` are unaffected and in use.

| Script | What | Undo |
|---|---|---|
| `install-mackeys` | no root: installs `mackeys.lua` into the Hyprland config | `--remove` |
| `mackeys.lua` | the shortcut definitions | n/a |
| `mac-key-extras` | choose which of ⌘W ⌘T ⌘F ⌘S ⌘L ⌘G ⌘P also work in apps (`W T F S`, `all`, `none`); in terminals they keep their Omarchy meaning, and the Omarchy action stays reachable at a new chord in every window | `mac-key-extras none` |
| `install-keyd` | **root.** Installs keyd and the Mac command layer below, plus the `keyd-appmap` service; `--dry-run` previews every step and prints the configuration without sudo; `--caps-delay MS` | `sudo install-keyd --remove` |
| `keyd-config` | prints the keyd configuration, the app overlays, the Super-chord table and the Apple keyboards it finds; changes nothing | n/a |
| `keyd-appmap` | the service that tells terminals from apps (see below) | removed by `install-keyd --remove` |
| `caps-lock` | no root: `real` (a Mac-style Caps Lock) or `compose` (Omarchy's default) | `caps-lock compose` |

## Which one do I want?

| | `mackeys.lua` | the keyd layer |
|---|---|---|
| Root | no | once (a service and a package) |
| Which ⌘ shortcuts | the 13 listed, plus the opt-in extras | every key: ⌘C ⌘T ⌘W ⌘F ⌘L ⌘1…9 and the rest are plain Ctrl |
| ⌘-click, ⌘-scroll, ⌘-drag | no (a bind sees keys, not the pointer) | yes: Ctrl is really held |
| Terminals | skipped | ⌘C copies, ⌘V pastes, ⌘K clears, ⌘W closes; the dangerous Ctrl chords are blocked |
| What it costs | nothing | the left ⌘ key is no longer Super (the right one is) |

They coexist. `mackeys.lua` keeps serving the right ⌘ key (a Hyprland bind sees Super, so right ⌘+Z is still undo) and is the fallback if keyd is never installed. With the
keyd layer the opt-in extras (`mac-key-extras`) are not needed: ⌘W, ⌘T, ⌘F, ⌘S, ⌘L, ⌘G and ⌘P are already plain Ctrl in apps.

## The keyd layer

Only Apple keyboards (found in `/proc/bus/input/devices`, written as `k:vendor:product`; the `k:` keeps the trackpad, which has the same id, out of it) are remapped. An external
PC keyboard keeps its keys. Nothing else about Ctrl, Option or the right ⌘ key changes.

| You press | Apps receive | Note |
|---|---|---|
| ⌘ + any key not listed below | Ctrl + that key | ⌘T ⌘W ⌘F ⌘L ⌘R ⌘A ⌘Z ⇧⌘Z ⇧⌘T ⌘1…9 … |
| ⌘C / ⌘V | Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V (Ctrl+Insert / Shift+Insert until the helper runs) | the helper switches them, see Terminals |
| ⌘← / ⌘→ | Home / End | ⇧ extends the selection |
| ⌘↑ / ⌘↓ | Ctrl+Home / Ctrl+End | top and bottom of the document |
| ⌥← / ⌥→ | Ctrl+← / Ctrl+→ | move by words (also on the right ⌥) |
| ⌥⌫ / ⌥⌦ | Ctrl+Backspace / Ctrl+Delete | delete a word (a terminal keeps Alt+Backspace) |
| ⌘[ / ⌘] | Alt+← / Alt+→ | back and forward |
| ⇧⌘[ / ⇧⌘] | Ctrl+Shift+Tab / Ctrl+Tab | previous and next tab |
| ⌥⌘I / ⌥⌘J / ⌥⌘C / ⌥⌘U | Ctrl+Shift+I / J / C, Ctrl+U | developer tools, console, inspect, view source |
| ⌥⌘← / ⌥⌘→ | Ctrl+PageUp / PageDown | previous and next tab |
| ⇧⌘. | Ctrl+H | show hidden files in Files |

These ⌘ chords are Mac *system* chords, so they go to Hyprland as **Super chords**; `keyd-config chords` prints the table, and the Hyprland side has to bind the ones marked "to bind":

| You press | Hyprland receives | Today in Omarchy |
|---|---|---|
| ⌘Space | Super+Alt+Space | Apps menu (searchable) |
| ⌘Tab / ⇧⌘Tab | Super+Tab / Super+Shift+Tab, with Super held until ⌘ is released | next / previous workspace |
| ⌘` and, while the switcher is up, ← → | Super+grave; Super+Shift+Tab, Super+Tab | unbound |
| ⌘Q / ⌘H / ⌘M | Super+Q / Super+H / Super+M | unbound |
| Esc while the switcher is up | Super+Alt+Escape (never Super+Esc, which is Omarchy's system menu) | unbound |
| ⇧⌘3 / ⇧⌘4 / ⇧⌘5 | Shift+Print / Print / Super+Ctrl+C | Shift+Print unbound; Print is the screenshot; the capture menu |
| ⌃⌘Q / ⌃⌘Space / ⌃⌘F | Super+Ctrl+L / Super+Ctrl+E / Super+F | lock, emoji picker, full screen |
| ⌘W / ⌘N in a terminal | Super+W / Super+Return | close window / new terminal |

**Super stays held for the app switcher.** After the first ⌘Tab, keyd keeps Super pressed (and not Ctrl) until ⌘ is released, so a switcher bound to Super+Tab can see ⌘ being released and
commit, exactly like a Mac. Verified against keyd's engine (see below).

### Terminals

A terminal reads Ctrl+C as "interrupt", Ctrl+D as "end of input", Ctrl+Z as "stop", Ctrl+S as "freeze". On a Mac none of those is ⌘'s business, so a terminal must never receive ⌘ as
Ctrl+letter. keyd's own `keyd-application-mapper` speaks X, Sway and GNOME but not Hyprland, so `keyd-appmap` does the same job here: it listens on Hyprland's event socket, asks the
compositor whether the focused window carries Omarchy's `terminal` tag (so a terminal added to Omarchy's rule works here too), and applies one of two overlays with `keyd bind`:

- **app:** ⌘C = Ctrl+C, ⌘V = Ctrl+V (a file manager does not take Ctrl+Insert). A launcher, a menu or no window at all counts as an app.
- **terminal:** ⌘C = Ctrl+Insert, ⌘V = Shift+Insert, ⇧⌘C / ⇧⌘V = Ctrl+Shift+C / V, ⌘K clears, ⌘W closes the window, ⌘N opens a terminal, ⌘. = Ctrl+C (as in Terminal and iTerm),
  ⌥⌫ = Alt+Backspace, and ⌘A ⌘B ⌘D ⌘E ⌘F ⌘G ⌘I ⌘J ⌘O ⌘P ⌘R ⌘S ⌘T ⌘U ⌘X ⌘Y ⌘Z do nothing. Physical Ctrl still sends every one of them, the way a Mac's Control does.

**It fails closed.** If the service is down, keyd falls back to its static configuration, which is the terminal-safe one: ⌘C and ⌘V are Ctrl+Insert and Shift+Insert, which GTK, Chromium and
every Omarchy terminal accept (a file manager may ignore them: copy then does nothing, which is a nuisance and not a danger). The remaining Ctrl+letter chords (⌘D, ⌘Z) would reach a shell
until the service is back; systemd restarts it after 2 seconds.

**Why a root service and not the `keyd` group.** `keyd bind` needs the keyd socket. A user in the `keyd` group can make keyd run commands as root, so the group is root-equivalent for everything
in the session (a browser tab included). The service runs as root instead, with only the two capabilities it needs to read the session's sockets, no network, no home directories and a
read-only file system; it takes its bindings from a root-owned file, and from the focused window it uses a single bit: terminal or not. It refuses sockets that are symlinks or not
owned by the session's user.

### Caps Lock

With the keyd layer Caps Lock needs a deliberate press of 150 ms, as on a Mac (a quick brush does nothing; `--caps-delay 0` turns that off). Apple does not publish the delay, so 150 ms is an
estimate: tune it with `sudo install-keyd --caps-delay MS`. The light on the key should follow Caps Lock (keyd passes the light's state on, which was read in its source and not tried on this keyboard).

### Install, preview, undo

```bash
~/labspace/omarchy-kit/keys/install-keyd --dry-run     # no sudo: every step, and the configuration it would write
sudo ~/labspace/omarchy-kit/keys/install-keyd          # install (keyd package, /etc/keyd/omarchy-kit-mac.conf, the service)
sudo ~/labspace/omarchy-kit/keys/install-keyd --remove # undo; the keyd package stays (sudo pacman -Rns keyd removes it)
```

It refuses (and changes nothing) if keyd's own `keyd check` rejects the configuration, if another keyd configuration exists (a keyboard can be in only one file), if there is no Apple keyboard,
or if it was not started with sudo from your own account. Running it twice changes nothing.

After installing: press Caps Lock briefly (nothing), then hold it a moment (the light comes on); try ⌘C and ⌘V in Brave, in Files and in a terminal (in the terminal ⌘C must copy, not
interrupt a running program); try ⌘←, ⌥← and ⌘[ in a text field. Left ⌘ no longer starts Omarchy's Super shortcuts: use the right ⌘ key (or the trackpad gestures for spaces).

### Limits

- Written for an ANSI keyboard: the `` ` `` key is the one left of the 1 key. An ISO keyboard needs `102nd` bound as well.
- ⌘← and ⌘→ are Home and End, which on a web page scroll to the top and the bottom; a Mac's browsers use them for back and forward (use ⌘[ and ⌘]).
- `sudo keyd reload` drops the overlays until the focus next changes (the installer restarts the service, so this only matters if you reload by hand).
- Only the physical Apple keyboards are remapped. Typing through fcitx5 or a virtual keyboard (wtype) is not.

### How it was checked

`test/test_keyd.py` (about 7 seconds). Always: the generator, the helper against fake Hyprland sockets and a fake keyd, the installer run as fake root in a private namespace (install, again, remove twice,
refusals, the unit through `systemd-analyze verify`), `caps-lock`. With `KEYD_BIN=/path/to/keyd`: keyd's own `keyd check` on every configuration the generator can write. With `KEYD_SRC=/path/to/keyd/source`
(and gcc): `test/keyd-trace.c` links keyd's real engine, and 17 tests feed it key events and compare the keys that come out (every chord above, the switcher hold, both overlays, the Caps Lock delay).
Not checked without root and a physical keyboard: the daemon grabbing the device, how the keys feel, and the real length of a Caps Lock press.

## Caps Lock

Omarchy's default (`compose:caps,shift:both_capslock_cancel`) makes Caps Lock the **Compose key** (press, release, then `'` and `e` gives é) and moves Caps Lock to both Shift keys. `caps-lock real` empties
those options in a marked block at the end of `~/.config/hypr/input.lua` (the file as it was is kept once as `input.lua.bak-caps`): Caps Lock capitalises, the light on the key follows it, Shift does not cancel it.
What it removes: the Compose key and Caps Lock on both Shifts. The right Option key still types every accent (⌥e e = é). It keeps any other option Omarchy had (for example the Alt+Alt layout switch of
a non-Latin install), reloads Hyprland, restarts fcitx5 (it copies the keymap when it starts) and rebuilds the kit pages. `caps-lock compose` brings Omarchy's default back exactly.

## mackeys.lua

Verified against a real compositor: `node test/verify-mackeys.mjs` calls each handler through `hyprctl eval` and a scratch Brave window reports the exact chord it
receives (32 checks). Needs a running Hyprland session. Setup log rows: **⌘ shortcuts inside apps**, **⌘W ⌘T ⌘F ⌘S ⌘L ⌘G ⌘P in apps (optional)**, **Command works like on a Mac (keyd)**,
**Caps Lock is a real Caps Lock**.

---

FILE: icons/README.md  (icons/ scripts)
====================================================================================================

# icons/: Mac-style icons and pointer

> **TL;DR.** `install-icons` gives the desktop the macOS icon look: the WhiteSur icon theme (the closest free relative of the macOS icon style) and an
> open-source macOS pointer set. No root. It follows the light or dark mode of whichever Omarchy theme you pick, because a theme-set hook re-applies the
> right WhiteSur variant every time Omarchy changes theme (Omarchy would otherwise put its Yaru icons back). `--remove` undoes all of it.

| Command | What |
|---|---|
| `install-icons` | downloads two pinned releases, checks their checksums, installs the icons, the cursor, the hook and `maccursor.lua`, applies them now |
| `install-icons --remove` | removes only what it installed and puts Omarchy's own icon choice back |
| `mac-icons-hook` | the hook itself (installed as `~/.config/omarchy/hooks/theme-set.d/50-mac-icons`): light themes get `WhiteSur-light`, dark ones `WhiteSur-dark` |
| `maccursor.lua` | the Hyprland module (cursor theme and size); loaded from `hyprland.lua` |

## What it changes, and what it costs

- **Icons for every app that follows the system icon theme** (Files, the Omarchy menu, GTK and Qt apps, the Dock and the app switcher). Omarchy's Yaru
  folders and icons are replaced while this is installed. Apps that bring their own icons keep them.
- **The pointer** becomes the macOS arrow, hand and I-beam, at size 24. From the next login on in new sessions; `install-icons` also sets it live.
- **About 240 MB** under `~/.local/share/icons` (WhiteSur 124 MB, its dark and light variants 57 MB and 15 MB, two cursor sets 21 MB each).
- **Downloads** (GitHub, over HTTPS): WhiteSur tag `2026-09-10` and the `macOS` cursors `v2.0.1`. Both checksums are pinned in the script and the install stops,
  with nothing written, if either differs. Nothing from either project is stored in this repository.

## Honest limits

- **Not Apple's art.** macOS app icons are Apple's. WhiteSur is a community re-drawing in the same style (Big Sur era: rounded squares with a soft gradient); it
  does not reproduce the layered "Liquid Glass" icons of macOS 26 and 27. Nothing free does.
- **Coverage.** Of the 72 apps installed when this was written, WhiteSur drew 49. 19 more use icons that came with the app (mostly the Omarchy web apps) and 4
  (Kagi, Omarchy Kit, RetroArch, Tailscale) have none in any installed theme. The Dock and the switcher put every icon the theme does not have on a neutral
  rounded tile, which is what macOS does with apps that have not been given a new-style icon.
- **Fonts** are not changed. Apple's system font is not redistributable; GTK apps already use Adwaita Sans, a close free relative. See [MAC-FEEL](../docs/MAC-FEEL.md).

## How it was checked

- The install ran against the real desktop: both checksums matched, `gsettings` reported `WhiteSur-dark` and `macOS`, the Files window and the Dock showed
  the new icons in a screenshot.
- A real theme round trip (`mecha-unit` to `flexoki-light` and back): the icon theme went `WhiteSur-dark`, `WhiteSur-light`, `WhiteSur-dark`.
- `test/test_macdesktop.py` runs the installer in a sandbox with fake downloads: a wrong checksum installs nothing, an install is idempotent, `--remove` never
  deletes a folder it did not create, and the hook picks the right variant.

Undo: `icons/install-icons --remove`.

---

FILE: dock/README.md  (dock/ scripts)
====================================================================================================

# dock/: the Dock, the ⌘Tab app switcher and Mission Control

> **TL;DR.** A Mac-style Dock at the bottom of the screen and a ⌘Tab app switcher, in one small Quickshell program started with your session. The Dock
> has the magnification, the running dots, the bounce while an app launches, a right-click menu and the Downloads and Trash icons. ⌘Tab (Super+Tab) cycles
> through running apps, most recently used first, and letting go of ⌘ switches. F3 (the Mission Control key), Super+Ctrl+Up or four fingers up open **Mission Control**: every
> space across the top and the windows of the selected one, as real pictures of them, below. It follows the Omarchy theme's colours and the icon theme. No root; `install-dock --remove` undoes it.

| Command | What |
|---|---|
| `install-dock` | copies the program to `~/.local/share/macdock`, creates `~/.config/macdock/dock.json` if missing, adds the Hyprland module `macdock.lua` and starts the Dock |
| `install-dock --remove` | stops it and removes the program and the module; **your `dock.json` stays** |
| `quickshell -p ~/.local/share/macdock` | run it by hand in a terminal to see its log (stop the running one first) |
| `quickshell ipc -p ~/.local/share/macdock call dock toggleAutohide` | hide or show the Dock (also ⌥⌘D, Super+Alt+D) |

## The Dock

| Part | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Pinned apps, then the other running apps after a separator, then Downloads and Trash | the first group is `pinned` in `dock.json` (desktop file ids; ones that are not installed are skipped) |
| Hover | the icon under the pointer grows (magnification), its neighbours spread, its name shows above it. The grown icon stays under the pointer |
| Click | focuses the app (its most recently used window), or launches it with a bounce until its window appears; middle click opens a new instance |
| Right click | the app's windows, its own actions (New Window and so on), **Keep in Dock** / **Remove from Dock**, **Quit** |
| Dot under an icon | the app has a window (hidden ones too) |
| Web apps | Omarchy's web apps (WhatsApp, Omarchy Kit, ...) are matched to their launcher, so the pinned icon lights up instead of a second icon appearing |
| Icons the theme does not have | set on a neutral rounded tile, like macOS does for old-style icons |
| Trash | full icon when there is something in it; right click: Open, Empty Trash |

`~/.config/macdock/dock.json`: `pinned` (list), `iconSize` (32-96, default 52), `zoom` (1 = no magnification, default 1.6), `autohide` (default false),
`showTrash` (default true). It is re-read when it changes. With `autohide` the Dock slides away and the windows get its space back (85 px at the default size).

## ⌘Tab and the app shortcuts

| Keys | What | What it replaced |
|---|---|---|
| Super+Tab, Super+Shift+Tab | the app switcher, forwards and backwards. Hold Super, press Tab to step, let go to switch. Also: arrows, Return, Esc (cancel), **Q** quits the selected app, **H** hides it | they were *Next / Previous workspace* |
| Super+Ctrl+Shift+Right, Left | next / previous workspace | (moved here; three- and four-finger swipes and Super+1..9 still work) |
| ``Super+` `` | the next window of the same app | free |
| Super+Q | quit the app: closes every window of the focused app (apps that ask about unsaved work still ask) | free |
| Super+H | hide the app: its windows go to a hidden workspace; clicking it in the Dock or picking it in the switcher brings them back | free |
| Super+M | hide this one window (the nearest tiling has to "minimise") | free |
| Super+Alt+D | hide or show the Dock | free |
| F3, Super+Ctrl+Up, four fingers up on the trackpad | **Mission Control** (see below). F3 is the Mac keyboard's Mission Control key; it produced `XF86LaunchA`, which nothing was bound to | free; the swipe used to open the Omarchy menu |
| F4 | the **Apps menu**, like a four-finger pinch (F4 is the Mac keyboard's Launchpad key; it produced `XF86LaunchB`, which nothing was bound to; macOS 26 replaced Launchpad with an Apps view) | free |
| Super+Ctrl+Down | **App Exposé**: only the windows of the focused app, from every space | free |

"Super" is the ⌘ key on this keyboard. With the keyboard remap in [keys/](../keys/README.md) the left ⌘ sends these chords for you.

## Mission Control and App Exposé

F3, Super+Ctrl+Up or a four-finger swipe up opens a full-screen overview over the dimmed wallpaper: a **Spaces bar** with one card per workspace ("Desktop 1",
"Desktop 2", ..., the apps on it as small icons, the current one outlined, a **+** at the end), and below it the windows of the selected space, scaled to fit in rows
with their real proportions, each with its app icon and title. The previews are **real pictures of the windows**, taken once when the overview opens (not live), including
windows on spaces you are not looking at.

| Do | Result |
|---|---|
| click a window | go to it (and to its space) and close the overview |
| click a space card | show that space's windows; double-click it (or press Return on it) to go there |
| click **+** | go to the next empty space |
| hover a window, click the **x** at its corner | close that window; the others re-flow |
| arrows | Left and Right move along a row, Up and Down move between the Spaces bar and the windows and between rows of windows; Return does what a click does |
| Esc, a click on empty space, F3 again or the same swipe again | close it |

App Exposé (Super+Ctrl+Down) shows the focused app's windows only, from every space, with the space number after each title. Windows hidden with Super+H are not shown in either.

Cost, measured on this laptop: nothing is mapped or captured while it is closed (the Dock program stays at 0.10 % of one core and about 255 MB); opening takes about a quarter of a
second and one second of CPU time, adds about 75 MB while it is open, and the memory goes back when it closes. Held open it uses no CPU: there is no live capture. It is one surface
on the primary screen; on several monitors it covers the one it opens on and lists the windows of all of them.

## What it does not do (yet)

- No drag to reorder or to drag an icon out; reorder by editing `pinned`.
- No minimised windows in the Dock (hidden ones keep the app's dot), no badges, no live window previews in the switcher.
- Mission Control cannot drag a window onto another space's card, has no animation from the real window to its card (it fades in), and shows the picture of the window as it was when it
  opened. A window that cannot be captured shows its app icon on a dark card instead (none failed in the tests).
- No real blur behind the glass. Hyprland's blur costs GPU time on this laptop's Intel graphics at 2880x1800, so the glass is a tinted, translucent surface (the
  switcher and menus are nearly opaque so text behind them cannot be read through them). It is a decision to measure before changing, not a missing line.
- Bottom only (no left or right Dock).

## How it was checked

On the real desktop (screenshots of the real compositor, not a simulation):

- Magnification, names, running dots, extra apps after the separator, autohide on and off (the reserved space went 85 px to 0 and back), light and dark
  themes (a real round trip through `flexoki-light`).
- The switcher: opened over three apps, Tab moved the selection, Return switched, and releasing Ctrl or Super committed (key events sent with `wtype` while the
  switcher had the keyboard).
- ``Super+` ``, `Super+Q`, hide and restore, on real Files and Obsidian windows, driven through `hyprctl eval`.
- Mission Control, on real windows spread over three spaces (this terminal and Files on space 1, Obsidian on 2, Disks on 3): screenshots with real previews of windows on the visible and
  on the other spaces; the global shortcut that F3 and the swipe send opens and closes it; Esc, the arrow keys (between the bar and the windows, along the cards), Return and Left/Right
  sent as real key events while it had the keyboard; Return on a window of another space switched to that space and focused it; the **x** (through a test hook) closed a window and
  re-flowed the cards; **+** went to workspace 4; App Exposé listed the two Files windows from two spaces; the layout function is run in `node` by the tests (proportions kept, nothing
  overlaps or leaves the screen, up to eleven windows).
- Web apps: a real Omarchy Kit window lit the pinned icon.
- `test/test_macdesktop.py`: the installer in a sandbox (files, `dock.json` kept, one require line, clean removal), QML and Lua syntax, and that every QML file is installed.

**Not verified, because it needs a real keyboard or pointer:** pressing the actual F3, Super+Ctrl+Up, Super+Ctrl+Down and Super+Tab chords, the real four-finger swipe (the swipe handler runs the same
global shortcut as F3, which was tested; the gesture itself was not), hovering to show the close button and clicking cards (the same code runs through the tested IPC calls), Mission Control in a light theme
(it uses the same theme colours as the Dock), pressing the actual Super+Tab chord (Hyprland ignores `wtype`'s virtual keyboard for key binds, and the
release watcher uses `hl.is_key_down`, which does not see it either), mouse clicks and right-click menus (no pointer injection here), and starting at login
(`hyprland.start`). The checklist for those is on the Setup log page.

## Files

`shell.qml` (entry), `Dock.qml`, `DockIcon.qml`, `ItemMenu.qml`, `Switcher.qml`, `MissionControl.qml`, `AppIcon.qml`, `Apps.qml` (what is running, pinned and hidden), `Config.qml`
(`dock.json`), `Theme.qml` (colours from the Omarchy theme), `IconIndex.qml` (which icons the theme has), `macdock.lua` (the Hyprland side), `install-dock`.

Undo: `dock/install-dock --remove`.

FILE: menubar/README.md  (menubar/ scripts)
====================================================================================================

# menubar/: the Mac menu bar

> **TL;DR.** Omarchy's top bar rearranged the way macOS lays out its menu bar: a system menu (Apple menu) and the **name of the focused app in bold** at the left, then File, Edit,
> View, Window and Help menus; the workspaces in the middle; the status icons and the clock at the right. Almost no Wayland app publishes a real menu, so these are the
> standard Mac menus and each item sends the matching ⌘ shortcut to the focused app. No root; your original bar layout is saved and `--remove` restores it exactly.

| Command | What |
|---|---|
| `install-menubar` | adds the "Mac menu bar" widget to the bar, installs `macmenu.lua`, saves your layout, then rearranges the bar |
| `install-menubar --remove` | restores the saved layout, removes the widget and the module |
| `omarchy-shell omarchykit.macmenu open edit` | open a menu without the pointer (`apple`, `app`, `file`, `edit`, `view`, `window`, `help`); `close`, `current`, `activate <id>` also exist |

## What you get

| Menu | Items (each does what its ⌘ shortcut does in the focused app) |
|---|---|
| Omarchy logo (Apple menu) | About This Mac (the kit's MacBook page), System Settings, Software, Omarchy Menu, Force Quit, Sleep, Restart, Shut Down, Lock Screen, Log Out |
| App name (bold) | Settings (⌘,), Hide (⌘H), Quit (⌘Q) |
| File | New Window ⌘N, New Tab ⌘T, Open ⌘O, Close ⌘W, Save ⌘S, Print ⌘P |
| Edit | Undo ⌘Z, Redo ⇧⌘Z, Cut ⌘X, Copy ⌘C, Paste ⌘V, Select All ⌘A, Find ⌘F, Find Next ⌘G |
| View | Reload ⌘R, Zoom In, Zoom Out, Actual Size, Enter Full Screen |
| Window | Float or Tile, Center, Move to Workspace 1 to 5, Next Window of This App, the app's open windows |
| Help | Omarchy Kit, Keyboard Shortcuts |

Moving across the titles while a menu is open switches menus, as on a Mac. The bar keeps its transparency; the clock keeps its format (`Fri 23 Oct 00:36`).

## The honest part: these are not the app's own menus

A real global menu needs a menu service on the desktop and every app to publish its menu to it. No such service runs on this desktop, and as far as I could find Brave, Chromium
and Electron apps have no way to publish one on Wayland, so there is nothing real to show for most of the apps in the Dock. What this does instead is the same job at its most useful: the
menus teach and run the shortcuts. The shortcuts are the common ones, so an app that uses different keys for something (a terminal, a game) can ignore an item. In terminals Copy and
Paste are translated to the terminal's own keys and Close closes the window.

## What the installer changes in the bar

| Before (Omarchy's default arrangement) | After |
|---|---|
| left: Omarchy menu button, workspaces | left: the Mac menu bar widget |
| centre: indicators, clock, keyboard layout, weather, updates | centre: workspaces |
| right: tray, network, audio, power, ... | right: the same, plus indicators, updates, weather and keyboard layout, ending with the clock |

Anything else you had in the bar (extra widgets, spacers, custom command modules) keeps its place on the right, before the clock, with its settings. The Omarchy menu button is gone from the
bar (the Apple menu has an *Omarchy Menu* item and Super+Space still opens it). Your layout before the change is saved in `~/.config/omarchy-kit/menubar-layout-before.json`
and `shell.json.bak-menubar` is a plain copy of the file; `--remove` puts the layout back exactly.

## Notes

- After the **plugin code** changes (not the layout), restart the shell once: `omarchy restart shell`. Omarchy reloads a placed widget's files but does not rebuild the widget that is already on screen.
- `⌘Q` and `⌘H` in these menus use the Dock module (`dock/install-dock`); without it those two items do nothing.

## How it was checked

On the real desktop: a screenshot of the new bar, the Edit menu and the Apple menu open (dark and light themes); `File > New Window` opened a second Files window
and the menu closed (menu to `hyprctl eval` to the app); the window actions (Ctrl+N, Ctrl+W, quit) on real Files windows. `test/test_macdesktop.py`: the layout moves to the Mac order and back
to the exact original, nothing the user had is lost or duplicated, invalid `shell.json` is never touched, and every item id in the widget has a Lua action.
**Not verified:** pointer clicks and hover-to-switch (no pointer injection here); they use the same code paths as the tested `open` and `activate` calls.

Undo: `menubar/install-menubar --remove`.

FILE: look/README.md  (look/ scripts)

# look/: the Mac details that are not a theme

> **TL;DR.** `install-look` gives the Omarchy shell (bar, menus, panels) and the Dock a proportional UI font like macOS's San Francisco, moves the window close button of GTK apps to the left like the red
> traffic light, and installs the switch for **blur behind the glass** (off until you turn it on with `mac-glass on`). No root; `--remove` undoes it all. The corners, shadows, popups and colours of the Golden Gate look are in the two
> themes, [Golden Gate and Golden Gate Night](../themes/golden-gate/THEME.md), not here.

| Command | What |
|---|---|
| `install-look` | the font rule, the window-button layout, the glass module; restarts the Omarchy shell once (a couple of seconds) |
| `install-look --remove` | removes them and puts your previous button layout back exactly |
| `mac-glass on`, `mac-glass off`, `mac-glass status` | blur behind the Dock, switcher, Mission Control, menus, notifications and launcher (and the drop-downs of the bar, but not the bar itself) |

## What each part does and costs

- **UI font** (`60-kit-mac-ui-font.conf`, installed in `~/.config/fontconfig/conf.d/`). The Omarchy shell draws everything in the system *monospace* font and gives themes no way to change that. This
  fontconfig rule applies only to programs named `quickshell` (the shell and the Dock) and only to requests for the monospace alias: they get **Adwaita Sans** (GNOME's UI font, derived from Inter, the closest free
  relative of San Francisco). Terminals, editors and every other program keep their monospace font; the `sans-serif` alias and the shell's icon font are untouched (checked with `fc-match` in the tests). Apple's own font
  cannot be redistributed. Needs a shell restart to take effect (the installer does it).
- **Window buttons on the left** (`org.gnome.desktop.wm.preferences button-layout`, from `appmenu:close` to `close:`). GTK and libadwaita apps such as Files then show the close button at the top left, where a
  Mac has it. Only close is shown: a tiling desktop has no minimise, and the green button's job (full screen) is a keyboard shortcut here. Your previous value is saved once in `~/.config/omarchy-kit/look-saved.conf`.
- **Glass** (`macglass.lua`, loaded from `hyprland.lua`). Off by default. `mac-glass on` turns on Hyprland's blur and a layer rule that blurs the shell's own surfaces; windows keep their opacity and are not blurred. It costs GPU time, and on
  this laptop's Intel graphics at 2880x1800 that means heat: see the measurement in [MAC-FEEL](../docs/MAC-FEEL.md#blur-behind-the-glass) before deciding to leave it on. The state is one word in `~/.config/omarchy-kit/glass`.

## How it was checked

- The bar redrawn with the font rule on the real desktop (screenshot): proportional text, every icon still drawn, the clock and the Mac menu bar in the same font.
- `test/test_macsweep.py`: the rule is well-formed and narrow (and, with fontconfig, changes monospace for `quickshell` only), `install-look` in a sandbox with a fake `gsettings` that remembers (install, twice,
  `--remove` restores the layout exactly), `mac-glass` argument handling and its state file, the module parses and never blurs the bar itself.
- **Not verified:** the effect of `mac-glass on` on battery life (see MAC-FEEL), and the button layout in a real Files window (no pointer to click it; the setting itself is read back).

Undo: `look/install-look --remove`.

---
